rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four genuinely different press shapes, including the sharp infrastructure angle: "Reimbursing an employee in local currency in 50 countries is a regulatory problem before it is a product." B is competent, but it pads two versions of the same customer-globalization story, especially "Brex's global card rollout is a bet that expense software has to go everywhere its customers do" and "The corporate-card feature CFOs of global startups actually asked for." A also shows more discipline by refusing remote-work/customer-story bait instead of smuggling it into the kept angles. That is the difference between a strategist and a deck generator wearing a tie.
gaps_in_A: "means dozens of regulatory and banking arrangements" is plausible, but still an inference from the update; it needs a softer phrasing or explicit proof before pitching.
"international issuing is expensive to build and operate" is likely true, but the update gives no cost data, so the funding-mechanics angle must stay framed as scrutiny, not assertion.
The enterprise-demand angle rests heavily on Brex's own "top enterprise customer request" claim; without one named buyer or methodology, it can wobble.
gaps_in_B: "not a phased pilot" is invented. The update says a 50-country launch, not that it is all live at once with no phased rollout.
"distributed teams" appears repeatedly, but the supplied facts do not tie the launch to remote or distributed work. That is exactly the kind of easy story a reporter will fact-check into dust.
"The corporate-card feature CFOs of global startups actually asked for" overreaches: no CFOs, no named global startups, and no customer quote were supplied.
The first and third kept angles are too close: both are versions of "customers went global, so Brex followed." One should be replaced with the plumbing/regulatory story B missed.
